transitivity: both — transitive (help a neighbor), intransitive (a short nap helps)
gloss: To make something easier or better for someone.
examples: Could you *help* me with these bags?
My neighbors *helped* us for weeks after the flood.
She has been *helping* at the shelter every Saturday.
contrast: *Help* takes a bare infinitive or *to*: *help me carry it* or *help me to carry it* — never *help me carrying it*.

transitivity: both — transitive (assist the doctor), intransitive (assist with the move)
gloss: To help someone, usually with part of a job or task.
examples: Two aides *assist* the teacher every morning.
A stranger *assisted* her with the stroller.
He is *assisting* in the search for the missing hiker.
contrast: *Assist* someone **with** something or **in** doing something, not *assist to do*.

gloss: To give help or support to someone who needs it.
examples: Volunteers *aid* families after every storm.
Rest and water *aided* his recovery.
Hundreds of people have been *aided* by the new clinic.
contrast: Sounds exactly like the noun *aide* (an assistant): *the nurse's aide aided the patient*.

gloss: To make a process easier or help it happen smoothly.
examples: Small grants *facilitate* access to childcare.
She *facilitated* the meeting between the two families.
The new app is *facilitating* donations from all fifty states.

transitivity: both — transitive (the law obliges us to report it), intransitive (she asked, and he obliged)
gloss: To do a favor that someone has asked for, or to make someone do something.
examples: He always *obliges* when a neighbor needs a ride.
She asked for one more song, and the pianist *obliged*.
Doctors are *obliged* to report certain injuries.
contrast: *Obliged* also means grateful — *I'd be much obliged*.

gloss: To support someone or something, or to treat one side better than another.
examples: Most parents *favor* the new after-school program.
The coach openly *favored* his own son.
She has always *favored* the youngest of her grandchildren.
contrast: American spelling has no *u*: *favor, favored*; British English writes *favour, favoured*.

transitivity: both — transitive (engage the students), intransitive (engage with the community)
gloss: To draw someone into an activity or conversation, or to take an active part in something.
examples: Good tutors *engage* every child in the room.
The center *engaged* two hundred volunteers last year.
She has been *engaging* with families who are afraid to ask for help.
contrast: For the sense of taking part, use *engage **with***: *engage with the community*.

gloss: To join with another person or organization to work toward the same goal.
examples: Local churches *partner* with the food bank every winter.
We *partnered* with a clinic to offer free checkups.
They are *partnering* on a program for new mothers.
contrast: *Partner **with*** someone, never *partner to*.

gloss: To support a person, plan, or cause, especially with money or public approval.
examples: Several donors *back* the food pantry.
The city council *backed* her proposal last night.
The shelter is *backed* by one small family foundation.

gloss: To help something move forward or succeed.
examples: Scholarships *further* the careers of young nurses.
Her testimony *furthered* the cause more than any ad.
They are *furthering* the work their founder began.
contrast: The verb is *further*; *farther* is only about physical distance.

gloss: To strengthen or support something that has become weak.
examples: Kind words *bolster* a child's confidence.
The donation *bolstered* the shelter's budget.
Extra staff have *bolstered* the night shift.

gloss: To support something by forming its base or foundation.
examples: Trust and patience *underpin* good caregiving.
Federal money *underpinned* the whole program.
The clinic is *underpinned* by hundreds of small donations.
contrast: The stress falls on *-pin*, so the *n* doubles: *underpinned, underpinning*.

gloss: To state formally that you support someone else's proposal.
examples: Someone has to *second* the motion before we vote.
She *seconded* his idea to open a warming center.
The proposal was *seconded* and passed the same evening.

ru: брать на себя, взять на себя (расходы, ответственность)
gloss: To accept a burden or cost so that other people do not have to.
examples: Older siblings often *shoulder* too much at home.
Her aunt *shouldered* the medical bills for a year.
He has *shouldered* the care of both parents alone.

gloss: To provide the people needed to run a place or service.
examples: Retired nurses *staff* the free clinic on weekends.
Volunteers *staffed* the phones all night.
The hotline is *staffed* around the clock.

gloss: To go with young people to an event in order to look after them.
examples: Two parents *chaperone* every field trip.
He *chaperoned* the eighth-grade dance.
She is *chaperoning* the trip to the museum tomorrow.
contrast: The *ch* is pronounced like *sh*; the word is also spelled *chaperon*.

transitivity: both — transitive (parent a teenager), intransitive (they parent very differently)
gloss: To raise and care for a child the way a parent does.
examples: The two of them *parent* very differently.
She *parented* three kids on her own.
He is *parenting* a teenager for the first time.

gloss: To care for someone in a protective, motherly way.
examples: She *mothers* every new volunteer.
His aunt *mothered* him for a year after the accident.
The older students are *mothering* the freshmen a little.

gloss: To raise and care for children or young animals until they grow up.
examples: They *rear* their children on a small farm.
She was *reared* by her grandmother.
He spent thirty years *rearing* horses.
contrast: *Rear* is the formal word; in everyday American speech people say *raise* a child.

ru: брать на воспитание (в приёмную семью); способствовать
gloss: To care for a child in your home without adopting, or to help something grow.
examples: They *foster* teenagers who are waiting for a permanent home.
The couple *fostered* six children over ten years.
The program is *fostering* trust between neighbors.

gloss: To treat someone with a great deal of comfort and attention.
examples: Grandparents love to *pamper* the little ones.
They *pampered* her for a week after the surgery.
He is being *pampered* by the whole family.

transitivity: both — transitive (indulge the kids), intransitive (indulge in dessert)
gloss: To let someone have whatever they want, or to allow yourself a pleasure.
examples: Aunts are supposed to *indulge* their nieces.
He *indulged* her every wish that Christmas.
They have been *indulging* the puppy shamelessly.
contrast: Use *indulge **in*** when people are treating themselves: *indulge in a second slice*.

gloss: To protect someone too much, in a way that keeps them weak.
examples: Some coaches *coddle* their best players.
His parents *coddled* him all the way through college.
She worries about *coddling* her youngest.

gloss: To go along with what someone wants in order to keep them happy.
examples: Nurses often *humor* patients who are confused.
We *humored* him and listened to the story again.
She was only *humoring* her little brother.
contrast: American spelling drops the *u*: *humor, humored*; British English writes *humour*.

transitivity: both — transitive (cuddle the baby), intransitive (cuddle on the couch)
gloss: To hold someone close in your arms to show affection or give comfort.
examples: Babies *cuddle* when they feel safe.
She *cuddled* the frightened puppy all evening.
They were *cuddling* under one blanket.

gloss: To settle into a warm, comfortable position close to someone.
examples: The kids *snuggle* up to their dad during storms.
She *snuggled* against her mother and fell asleep.
The cat is *snuggling* into the blanket.

gloss: To hold someone or something gently in your arms or hands.
examples: New parents learn how to *cradle* a newborn's head.
He *cradled* the injured bird until help came.
She is *cradling* the baby while she talks.

transitivity: both — transitive (rock the baby), intransitive (the chair rocks)
gloss: To move someone or something gently back and forth, often to calm them.
examples: Grandmothers *rock* babies to sleep.
He *rocked* her until the crying stopped.
She is *rocking* the baby in the old chair.

gloss: To develop a close emotional connection with someone.
examples: Foster parents and children need time to *bond*.
She *bonded* with the baby right away.
They have *bonded* over long nights at the hospital.
contrast: *Bond **with*** a person, or *bond **over*** a shared experience.

gloss: To give someone anxious, excessive attention, or (of a baby) to cry and complain.
examples: Stop *fussing* — I can carry my own bag.
She *fussed* over her guests all evening.
The baby *fusses* whenever he is tired.
contrast: *Fuss **over*** someone means to care for them anxiously.

gloss: To stroke an animal gently with your hand.
examples: Children may *pet* the goats at the farm.
She *petted* the old dog until he fell asleep.
He is *petting* the cat with one finger.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the *t* doubles: *petted, petting*.

gloss: To love someone so much that you give them constant, excessive attention.
examples: Grandparents *dote* on the first grandchild.
She *doted* on her little brother.
He has *doted* on that dog for twelve years.
contrast: Always *dote **on*** (or *upon*) someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (hydrate the patient), intransitive (hydrate before a run)
gloss: To give water to someone, or to drink enough water yourself.
examples: Nurses *hydrate* patients before surgery.
We *hydrated* the kids every twenty minutes in that heat.
She is *hydrating* after the long hike.

transitivity: both — transitive (rehydrate a sick child), intransitive (rehydrate slowly)
gloss: To replace the water that a person or animal has lost.
examples: Small sips *rehydrate* a sick child better than big ones.
The clinic *rehydrated* dozens of patients that week.
He is slowly *rehydrating* after the fever.

gloss: To give someone the food or care they need to stay healthy and grow.
examples: Warm meals *nourish* more than the body.
The program *nourished* two thousand children last winter.
She has been *nourishing* him back to health.

gloss: To treat someone with medicine.
examples: Doctors *medicate* only when it is really needed.
They *medicated* her for the pain.
He is being *medicated* for high blood pressure.

gloss: To give someone medicine or emergency treatment.
examples: Teachers may *administer* an EpiPen in an emergency.
A bystander *administered* first aid until the ambulance came.
The vaccine is *administered* in two doses.

gloss: To protect someone from a disease, usually with a vaccine.
examples: Clinics *immunize* children here for free.
The school *immunized* every student before the trip.
Most of the village has been *immunized*.
contrast: American spelling uses *-ize*: *immunize*; British English also allows *immunise*.

gloss: To put a vaccine into someone's body so that a disease cannot harm them.
examples: Doctors *inoculate* babies at two months.
The team *inoculated* four hundred people in a single day.
She was *inoculated* against measles as a child.
contrast: Spelled with one *n* and one *c*: *in-oc-u-late*.

gloss: To give someone a drug that makes them calm or sleepy.
examples: Vets usually *sedate* nervous dogs for X-rays.
They *sedated* him before setting the bone.
She was lightly *sedated* during the procedure.

gloss: To bring someone back to consciousness after their breathing or heart has stopped.
examples: Lifeguards train to *resuscitate* swimmers.
Paramedics *resuscitated* him at the scene.
The child was *resuscitated* and is doing well.
contrast: There is a silent *c* in the middle: *re-sus-ci-tate*.

ru: сортировать по срочности, проводить медицинскую сортировку
gloss: To decide which people or problems need attention first.
examples: Nurses *triage* everyone who walks into the ER.
Volunteers *triaged* the calls as they came in.
They are *triaging* patients in the hallway.

gloss: To keep a sick person away from others so that the illness does not spread.
examples: Hospitals *isolate* patients with the flu.
They *isolated* the whole family for ten days.
He is being *isolated* until the test comes back.

gloss: To protect someone or something from harm or loss.
examples: Strict rules *safeguard* the children in our care.
The money was *safeguarded* for emergencies.
They are *safeguarding* the records for these families.

gloss: To stop something bad from happening.
examples: Quick action can *avert* a tragedy.
A neighbor's phone call *averted* a disaster.
Several evictions have been *averted* by the fund.

gloss: To act early so that something bad cannot happen.
examples: Regular visits *forestall* a lot of problems.
The nurse *forestalled* a crisis by calling the family.
Hunger is being *forestalled* by the weekend meal bags.

ru: обеспечивать, гарантировать; позаботиться о том, чтобы
gloss: To make certain that something happens or is true.
examples: Two adults *ensure* that no child walks home alone.
The grant *ensured* that the clinic stayed open.
We are *ensuring* that every family gets a call.
contrast: *Ensure* = make certain; *insure* = buy insurance; *assure* = tell someone so they stop worrying.

gloss: To warn someone about a possible danger.
examples: Signs *caution* swimmers about the current.
The doctor *cautioned* her against lifting anything heavy.
Parents are being *cautioned* about the new app.
contrast: *Caution* someone **against** doing something, or **about** a danger.

transitivity: both — transitive (prep the patient), intransitive (prep for the exam)
gloss: To get a person or place ready for something.
examples: Nurses *prep* the patient before surgery.
We *prepped* the shelter for fifty guests.
She is *prepping* meals for her mother's whole week.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the *p* doubles: *prepped, prepping*.

ru: обезопасить для ребёнка, сделать безопасным для детей
gloss: To make a place or object safe for small children.
examples: New parents *childproof* every cabinet.
They *childproofed* the house before the twins arrived.
The playroom has already been *childproofed*.

gloss: To give someone a place to live or stay.
examples: The city *houses* families in an old motel.
The church *housed* twelve people that winter.
Refugee families are being *housed* by volunteers.
contrast: The verb ends in a *z* sound (HOWZ); the noun *house* ends in *s* (HOWS).

gloss: To give someone a temporary place to stay.
examples: Farms sometimes *lodge* seasonal workers.
A neighbor *lodged* them for three nights.
The hikers were *lodged* at the ranger station.

gloss: To give shelter to someone, often quietly or secretly.
examples: Some families still *harbor* runaway teenagers.
The farmhouse *harbored* refugees for months.
She has *harbored* stray cats for years.
contrast: American spelling has no *u*: *harbor*; British English writes *harbour*.

gloss: To watch over a place or activity in order to keep it safe and orderly.
examples: Parents *police* the group chat pretty closely.
Volunteers *policed* the crowd at the fair.
The playground is *policed* by two teachers at recess.

gloss: To check someone or something carefully before accepting or approving them.
examples: We *vet* every volunteer who works with kids.
The agency *vetted* the foster family for months.
All the drivers have been *vetted*.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the *t* doubles: *vetted, vetting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (brace his ankle), intransitive (brace for bad news)
gloss: To support something so it does not give way, or to get ready for something hard.
examples: Two straps *brace* his ankle.
The nurse *braced* him as he stood up.
They are *bracing* for a long winter at the shelter.

gloss: To give someone the official right to have or do something.
examples: Three years of service *entitle* you to paid leave.
The injury *entitled* her to free care.
Families are *entitled* to one visit a week.
contrast: *Entitle* someone **to** something: *entitled to help*, not *entitled for help*.

gloss: To free someone from a place or situation they are trapped in.
examples: Firefighters *extricate* drivers from wrecked cars.
They *extricated* the boy from the icy pond.
She is still *extricating* herself from that job.

gloss: To release someone from something that holds or limits them.
examples: Rescuers *free* animals caught in nets.
Neighbors *freed* the dog from the fence.
The money *freed* her from constant worry.
contrast: The *-ing* form keeps both *e*'s: *freeing*, and the past is *freed*, not *freeed*.

gloss: To protect someone from having to go through something unpleasant.
examples: Good neighbors *spare* you a lot of trouble.
She *spared* her mother the worst details.
He has been *spared* the paperwork this time.

gloss: To make pain or a problem less severe.
examples: Warm compresses *alleviate* the swelling.
A small grant *alleviated* their rent problem.
The new medicine is *alleviating* most of the pain.

gloss: To make the harmful effects of something less serious.
examples: Early visits *mitigate* the worst outcomes.
Insurance *mitigated* some of the loss.
They are *mitigating* the damage as best they can.

transitivity: both — transitive (lighten her load), intransitive (the mood lightened)
gloss: To make a load, worry, or duty easier to bear.
examples: Small favors *lighten* a caregiver's week.
Her sister *lightened* the load by taking two shifts.
The mood in the room is finally *lightening*.
contrast: The *-ing* form is *lightening* (making lighter); *lightning* in the sky has no *e*.

gloss: To correct something that is wrong or harmful.
examples: A hot meal will not *remedy* everything, but it helps.
The city *remedied* the heating problem in a week.
The shortage is being *remedied* by donations.
contrast: Consonant + *-y*, so the *y* becomes *i*: *remedies, remedied* — but *remedying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To soften the effect of something painful or difficult.
examples: Savings *cushion* a family against a bad month.
The grant *cushioned* the blow of the layoffs.
Her friends are *cushioning* her through the divorce.

gloss: To make someone who is angry or upset become calm.
examples: A bottle usually *pacifies* him.
She *pacified* the crying toddler with a song.
He spent the whole evening *pacifying* angry parents.
contrast: Consonant + *-y*: *pacifies, pacified*, but the *-ing* form keeps the *y*: *pacifying*.

gloss: To make someone less angry by doing or saying something kind.
examples: Apologies rarely *placate* a frightened patient.
The manager *placated* the family with a free room.
She is *placating* everyone while the repairs go on.

gloss: To calm someone by giving them some of what they want.
examples: Snacks *appease* the kids for about an hour.
He *appeased* his mother by agreeing to call every day.
The crowd was *appeased* by the announcement.

gloss: To make an unpleasant feeling less strong.
examples: Facts rarely *assuage* a parent's fear.
His calm voice *assuaged* her panic.
Their guilt has not been *assuaged* by the apology.

gloss: To make someone calm or sleepy, usually with gentle sound or movement.
examples: The rain *lulls* the baby every time.
She *lulled* him to sleep with an old song.
The engine noise was *lulling* the children.

transitivity: both — transitive (quiet the baby), intransitive (the ward quieted down)
gloss: To make someone calm and silent, or to become calm.
examples: A warm bottle will *quiet* him.
Her voice *quieted* the whole room.
The ward is *quieting* down for the night.
contrast: Americans say *quiet* (or *quiet down*); the British verb *quieten* is not used in the US.

gloss: To hold someone or something so that it does not shake or fall.
examples: A cane *steadies* him on the stairs.
She *steadied* her grandfather by the elbow.
He is *steadying* the ladder for her.
contrast: Consonant + *-y*: *steadies, steadied*, but *steadying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To show someone that you feel sorry about their trouble.
examples: Coworkers *commiserate* over bad news.
She *commiserated* with him about the diagnosis.
They were *commiserating* in the hallway.
contrast: *Commiserate **with*** a person **about** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (confide a secret), intransitive (confide in a friend)
gloss: To tell someone private things because you trust them.
examples: Teenagers rarely *confide* in a stranger.
She *confided* in her coach after the accident.
He has *confided* things he never told his parents.
contrast: *Confide **in*** the person you trust: *confide in her*, not *confide to her*.

gloss: To make someone feel more hopeful and cheerful.
examples: Small wins *hearten* the whole team.
The letters *heartened* her during treatment.
Donors have been *heartened* by the results.
contrast: The opposite is *dishearten*, to take someone's hope away.

gloss: To give someone the courage to do something.
examples: Kind teachers *embolden* shy students.
Her example *emboldened* other survivors to speak.
He was *emboldened* by their support.

gloss: To make someone feel happier and more hopeful.
examples: Simple visits *uplift* the residents.
The choir *uplifted* everyone in the room.
She felt *uplifted* after the meeting.
contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable (up-LIFT); the noun stresses the first (UP-lift).

gloss: To gently persuade someone to do something.
examples: Nurses *coax* him into eating a little.
She *coaxed* the frightened cat out from under the porch.
He is *coaxing* his father to use the walker.

gloss: To praise someone publicly for something they did well.
examples: We *commend* our volunteers at the end of each year.
The mayor *commended* the two teenagers who called 911.
She has been *commended* twice for bravery.
contrast: Do not confuse with *recommend*, which means to suggest something to someone.

gloss: To shock or excite people into taking action.
examples: Stories like hers *galvanize* a community.
The fire *galvanized* the whole town into helping.
Neighbors have been *galvanized* by the news.

gloss: To give someone new energy and enthusiasm.
examples: Good news *energizes* the volunteers.
The turnout *energized* the organizers.
The team is *energized* by the new director.

gloss: To wake someone up, or to stir them into action.
examples: Night nurses try not to *rouse* the patients.
The alarm *roused* the whole floor.
He was *roused* by his daughter's voice.

gloss: To encourage someone to act, or to make something happen faster.
examples: Deadlines *spur* people to donate.
Her illness *spurred* the family to move closer.
The campaign has *spurred* hundreds of new volunteers.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the *r* doubles: *spurred, spurring*.

gloss: To keep pushing someone gently to do something they are avoiding.
examples: Someone has to *prod* him to take his pills.
She *prodded* her husband into seeing a doctor.
The nurse has been *prodding* him to walk a little each day.
contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the *d* doubles: *prodded, prodding*.

transitivity: both — transitive (advocate change), intransitive (advocate for a patient)
gloss: To speak publicly in support of a person or cause.
examples: Parents *advocate* for their kids at every meeting.
She *advocated* for better care in nursing homes.
He has been *advocating* for foster teens since 2015.
contrast: The verb ends in *-kayt*; the noun *advocate* (a supporter) ends in *-kuht*.

gloss: To support and fight for a cause or a person you believe in.
examples: A few doctors *champion* home care for the elderly.
She *championed* the bill for two years.
The program has been *championed* by local families.

gloss: To ask people for money, help, or support.
examples: Churches *solicit* winter coats every November.
They *solicited* donations from every business on the block.
Funds are being *solicited* for the family.

gloss: To collect money for a charity or a cause.
examples: The students *fundraise* every spring.
They *fundraised* for months before the trip.
She has been *fundraising* since her son's diagnosis.

transitivity: both — transitive (canvass the neighborhood), intransitive (canvass for donations)
gloss: To go from person to person asking for support, money, or opinions.
examples: Volunteers *canvass* the neighborhood every fall.
They *canvassed* two hundred homes for the food drive.
He is *canvassing* his block for winter coats.
contrast: Two *s*'s in the verb *canvass*; *canvas* with one *s* is the heavy cloth.

gloss: To give a large sum of money that will support something permanently.
examples: Alumni *endow* scholarships for local students.
One family *endowed* the children's ward.
The clinic is *endowed* by a small foundation.

gloss: To give something valuable, especially as an honor.
examples: Few schools *bestow* that award on a volunteer.
The city *bestowed* its highest honor on the nurse.
The title has been *bestowed* only twice.
contrast: *Bestow* something **on** (or **upon**) someone.

gloss: To pay for something, especially over a long period.
examples: Two donors *bankroll* the whole after-school program.
Her uncle *bankrolled* the treatment.
The shelter is *bankrolled* by a single family.

transitivity: both — transitive (arbitrate a dispute), intransitive (arbitrate between roommates)
gloss: To settle an argument between two sides as a neutral judge.
examples: Counselors often *arbitrate* between roommates.
A retired judge *arbitrated* the dispute for free.
The case is being *arbitrated* next month.

gloss: To speak to someone on another person's behalf in order to help them.
examples: Teachers sometimes *intercede* with the principal.
Her aunt *interceded* with the landlord.
He has *interceded* for that family more than once.
contrast: *Intercede **with*** a person **for** (or **on behalf of**) someone.

gloss: To give care and attention to people who are in need.
examples: Chaplains *minister* to families in the ICU.
Neighbors *ministered* to the sick all winter.
She has been *ministering* to the homeless for years.
contrast: Always *minister **to*** someone; the stress stays on the first syllable, as in the noun.

gloss: To make it someone's legal or moral duty to do something.
examples: The law does not *obligate* you to help a stranger.
His promise *obligated* him to stay another month.
Nobody here is *obligated* to donate.
contrast: Americans say *obligated to*; *obliged to* sounds more British and more formal.

gloss: To guide and advise a less experienced person over a long period.
examples: Senior nurses *mentor* every new hire.
He *mentored* her through her first year of teaching.
She has been *mentoring* teenagers since college.

transitivity: both — transitive (tutor a student), intransitive (tutor after school)
gloss: To teach one student or a small group, usually outside of class.
examples: Retired teachers *tutor* kids at the library.
She *tutored* him in math all spring.
He is *tutoring* two refugee children in English.

transitivity: both — transitive (coach the team), intransitive (she coaches on weekends)
gloss: To train or advise someone so that they get better at something.
examples: Volunteers *coach* the youth team.
Her therapist *coached* her through the first week.
He has been *coaching* new parents for years.

gloss: To teach people, especially in order to give them knowledge they can use.
examples: Nurses *educate* families about home care.
The campaign *educated* thousands about the early signs.
Parents are being *educated* about the new rules.

transitivity: both — transitive (homeschool the kids), intransitive (they homeschool)
gloss: To teach your own children at home instead of sending them to school.
examples: Several families on this street *homeschool*.
They *homeschooled* their daughter for two years.
She is *homeschooling* while her son recovers.

gloss: To give someone the information they need before they act.
examples: Team leaders *brief* the volunteers each morning.
She *briefed* the family before the surgery.
We are being *briefed* at seven.

gloss: To talk with someone after an event to learn what happened and how they are doing.
examples: Counselors *debrief* the crew after every hard call.
They *debriefed* the volunteers that same night.
The team is being *debriefed* right now.

ru: ориентировать, вводить в курс; знакомить с обстановкой
gloss: To help someone get used to a new place or situation.
examples: Staff *orient* every new resident.
A volunteer *oriented* us on the first day.
New nurses are *oriented* for two weeks.
contrast: Americans say *orient*; *orientate* is the British form.

gloss: To help someone learn about something until they know it well.
examples: We *familiarize* every caregiver with the alarm system.
He *familiarized* himself with her medications.
They are *familiarizing* the kids with their new school.
contrast: *Familiarize* someone **with** something, not *to* something.

gloss: To give someone useful understanding of something they did not know.
examples: A good social worker can *enlighten* a frightened family.
She *enlightened* us about what the diagnosis really meant.
We were *enlightened* by the nurse's plain explanation.

gloss: To guide a group of people carefully from one place or stage to another.
examples: Aides *shepherd* the children across the street.
She *shepherded* the family through all the paperwork.
They are *shepherding* the group to the buses.
contrast: The middle *h* is silent: SHEP-urd.

gloss: To take careful responsibility for something that belongs to other people.
examples: Small charities have to *steward* every dollar.
The board *stewarded* the fund for decades.
The land is *stewarded* by the families who live on it.

transitivity: both — transitive (enroll her mother in day care), intransitive (enroll in a class)
gloss: To sign someone up officially for a program, school, or service.
examples: Caseworkers *enroll* families in the food program.
She *enrolled* her mother in adult day care.
Two hundred children have been *enrolled* this year.
contrast: American English doubles the *l*: *enroll*; British English writes *enrol*, though both make *enrolled, enrolling*.

gloss: To make someone part of a group or activity.
examples: Good teachers *include* every child in the game.
They *included* the new family in the holiday dinner.
He is finally being *included*.

gloss: To become a friend to someone, especially someone who is alone or in need.
examples: Volunteers *befriend* isolated seniors.
A classmate *befriended* him on his first day.
She has *befriended* three of the new arrivals.

transitivity: both — transitive (acclimate the new kids), intransitive (acclimate to the cold)
gloss: To get used to a new place or situation, or to help someone do that.
examples: It takes weeks to *acclimate* to a new country.
The family slowly *acclimated* to life here.
He is still *acclimating* to the altitude.
contrast: Americans say *acclimate*; the British form is *acclimatize*.

transitivity: both — transitive (reunite a child with her mother), intransitive (the family reunited)
gloss: To bring people together again after they have been apart.
examples: Agencies work to *reunite* children with their parents.
The shelter *reunited* the dog with its owner.
They were *reunited* after eleven years.

gloss: To give new strength and life to a person, place, or organization.
examples: New volunteers *revitalize* a tired program.
The grant *revitalized* the whole center.
The neighborhood is being *revitalized* by its own residents.

gloss: To help people move to a new place to live, usually after they have lost their home.
examples: Church groups *resettle* several families a year.
The agency *resettled* them in Ohio.
Thousands have been *resettled* since the spring.

gloss: To drive someone where they need to go.
examples: Grandparents often *chauffeur* the kids to practice.
He *chauffeured* his neighbor to chemo every Tuesday.
She has been *chauffeuring* her mother to appointments for a year.
contrast: French spelling, English sounds: *ch* is said like *sh*, and *-eur* rhymes with *fur*.

gloss: To speak to God, often asking for help for yourself or for someone else.
examples: Her whole church *prays* for the family every Sunday.
They *prayed* together in the waiting room.
She has been *praying* for his recovery for months.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *prey* (an animal that is hunted); the vowel + *y* keeps the *y*: *prayed*, not *praied*.

gloss: To give someone a measured amount of medicine.
examples: Parents *dose* children by weight, not by age.
The nurse *dosed* him again at midnight.
He has been *dosing* himself with cough syrup all week.
contrast: *Dose* ends in an *s* sound (DOHS); *doze*, to sleep lightly, ends in *z*.
